title: Large temporary cash transfers raised consumption and financial health without clear persistent net-worth gains
source_unit: U.S. low-income adults in a randomized three-year unconditional-cash-transfer experiment in two states

observations.period: Three-year transfer experiment; NBER Working Paper issued August 2024 and revised July 2025

denominator.unit: randomized individuals: 1,000 assigned to $1,000 monthly and 2,000 assigned to $50 monthly

monthly_transfer_contrast.unit: monthly difference between treatment and comparison assignment

household_expenditures.value: increased by at least $300 per month

spending_composition.value: positive effects in most categories, largest for housing, food, and car expenses

net_worth.unit: asset-value gains were offset by higher debt

financial_health.value: increased self-reported financial health and credit scores, without effects on credit limits, delinquencies, utilization, bankruptcies, or foreclosures

marginal_propensity_to_spend.value: 0.38–0.50 for nondurables and 0.18–0.24 for durables and semidurables; marginal propensity to delever near zero
marginal_propensity_to_spend.unit: dollars spent per dollar of transfer, reported adjusted estimates

observations.method: NBER Working Paper 32784 exploits random assignment to $1,000-per-month versus $50-per-month unconditional transfers for three years and examines consumption, balance sheets, and financial outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: This record retains the official abstract-level findings and reported ranges rather than reproducing the full analysis, attrition, survey response, or administrative linkage. The transfer is temporary and the sample is a young, low-income population in two states; observed financial-health improvements do not establish durable security or political response.
observations.subgroup: Young, low-income U.S. adults in the two-state randomized experiment; the abstract does not provide the full subgroup denominator or heterogeneity profile.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher spending and mobility can represent relief, catch-up consumption, housing repair, or displacement rather than durable asset accumulation. Near-zero net-worth effects and higher debt show why short-run financial health, consumption, and balance-sheet recovery must remain separate currencies.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI and working-paper metadata identify the study and authors.

boundary: This is a randomized U.S. transfer-to-consumption and balance-sheet result, not a universal cash-transfer effect or a complete household recovery, care, employment, trust, political-action, or long-run welfare estimate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER Working Paper 32784 page downloaded and hashed; title, date, random assignment, transfer contrast, spending, mobility, financial-health, debt, and net-worth findings checked against the abstract.
